records.table: Pisco Portón Mosto Verde Acholado is Peruvian pisco from Hacienda La Caravedo in Ica, distilled once from grape must before its fermentation ends and bottled at 43 per cent with no water added. Roses, mandarin and lime make it a perfumed Pisco Sour.
records.story: Pisco is the grape brandy of Peru's southern coast, and Hacienda La Caravedo in the Ica valley dates its own distilling to 1684, a date the house gives and travel guides repeat. The Portón label was made there in modern times, named for the Spanish word for a gate. It was built on the old Peruvian rules: eight pisco grapes, one distillation, no water to bring the strength down and no wood. Its mosto verde, distilled from must before it finishes fermenting, comes in seven single grapes and in the acholado blend. In the United States the tequila Patrón, whose name sounds close to Portón to an English ear, challenged the brand, and the American registration of the Portón name was cancelled in 2017. The house withdrew the name from that market, and the same distillery's piscos reached American shelves as Caravedo, while in Peru the bottle kept the Portón name. For a bartender it is the plain lesson in a Peruvian mosto verde: aromatic grapes, one pass through the still, and a strength reached at the still.

records.story: Bodega San Isidro stands in the Ica valley, on Peru's southern coast, and it is older than the label it makes: the house calls it a century old distillery, and the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails notes evidence of pisco made there in the nineteenth century. It had lain idle for decades when two Peruvian partners bought it in 2002 and brought it back to work, reconditioning the old buildings and keeping to the pot still method that, as the house tells it, Peru has followed since the sixteenth century. They called the pisco BarSol, and by 2005 it was going abroad, first among its range the pure Quebranta named Primero. The range grew to cover every style Peru's rules allow: puros of single grapes, an acholado that blends them, and mosto verde distilled from must before its fermentation ends. Newer labels print the pure Quebranta as BarSol Puro Quebranta, at the same strength. For a bartender it is the plain lesson in Quebranta, the non aromatic grape that gives Peruvian pisco its body, and a pisco made for the Pisco Sour.

records.story: Macchu Pisco was founded in 2006 by two Peruvian sisters, who built a label for Peruvian pisco made in the traditional way. Its name plays on Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel, spelt with a double c. The house began with Quebranta, the non aromatic grape that gives Peruvian pisco its earthy body, distilled once in copper pot stills in the valley of Ica and rested a year in vessels that give it nothing, as Peru's rules require, before it is bottled at the estate. Two siblings followed the plain bottling and between them show the other two Peruvian styles: La Diablada, an acholado named for an Andean dance in which angels fight devils, and Ñusta, a mosto verde named for the Quechua word for an Inca princess. The house filed American trade marks for both names in 2017. For a bartender the plain bottle is a clear lesson in a Quebranta pisco: pepper, citrus and earth where an Italia or a Torontel pisco would give flowers.

records.table: Capel Reservado is Chilean pisco from the growers' cooperative of the Elqui Valley, and its clear Transparente bottling is Pedro Jiménez grape, distilled twice and rested a year in steel, at 40 per cent. Light and clean, it is the pisco for a Piscola with cola.
records.story: Chile gave pisco a denomination of origin in 1931, reserving the name for the grape spirit of its northern regions of Atacama and Coquimbo. Seven years later, in February 1938, growers of the Elqui Valley, hit by the Depression and by more grapes than they could sell, joined together at Paihuano in a society that became a cooperative, its legal standing granted in 1939. In 1964 a reform of its statutes gave it the name Cooperativa Agrícola Pisquera Elqui, whose initials make Capel, and the Pisco Capel brand was launched that year. In 1967, with help from the state, it bought a distillery at Vicuña, in the Elqui Valley, which became its plant there. The cooperative went on to take in growers from across both pisco regions. In 1999 a decree set Chile's grades of pisco by strength, with Reservado at 40 per cent and above, and Chilean pisco may be distilled more than once, brought down with water and rested in wood. For a bartender Capel is the name that stands for Chilean pisco, and its Reservado teaches that Chile grades pisco by strength, not by age.

records.story: The Torres family of Penedès, in Catalonia, began distilling wine into brandy in 1928. In 1979 the family founded Miguel Torres Chile in the Curicó Valley, among the first foreign wine companies to settle in Chile. Its pisco came, by the house's own account, in 2012, eighty-four years after that first still in Penedès: Moscatel grapes from the Limarí Valley, in the Coquimbo region, distilled once in copper to keep their perfume. The name, the Governor, honours a man who fought for Chilean independence at the Battle of Maipú in 1818 and was later made governor of Ovalle, the town of the valley. The bottle entered a spirit that two countries claim. Chile reserves the name pisco to its Atacama and Coquimbo regions and allows more than one distillation, water and wood; Peru allows none of the three. El Gobernador keeps to a single distillation, as Peru does, and stays Chilean in its muscat perfume and its grade, Reservado, a strength of 40 per cent. For a bartender it is the clear lesson in an aromatic Chilean pisco.
